gold_direction: +precautionary (as to the weakness of the evidence base the Cass Review documented)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to what the Cass Review and its commissioned systematic reviews found)
question: What did the Cass Review (2024), the independent review of gender identity services for children and young people in England, conclude about the quality of the evidence for puberty blockers and masculinising/feminising hormones in adolescents?
required_claims: The University of York systematic reviews commissioned by Cass found a strikingly weak evidence base: of 50 studies of puberty blockers assessed (modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale), only 1 was rated high quality, 25 moderate, and 24 low

The reviews could draw no conclusions about the effects of puberty blockers on gender dysphoria, mental/psychosocial health, cognitive development, or fertility, and found that bone health and height may be compromised during treatment

The evidence for adolescent hormone therapy was similarly weak: essentially no high-quality studies and no adequate long-term follow-up, with only suggestive pre-post signals of possible psychological benefit

Cass's finding was an absence of a reliable evidence base — she did not find the treatments proven ineffective or proven harmful, and the review recommended providing care within a research framework rather than simply endorsing or banning routine use
acceptable_nuances: Cass also criticised the prevailing clinical culture: the 'time to think' rationale for blockers was undercut by the review's own finding that nearly all adolescents who started blockers proceeded to hormone therapy
Disagreement with the York reviews' quality thresholds exists, but the quality counts themselves are the reviews' documented output
forbidden_claims: The Cass Review proved puberty blockers and hormones are harmful or ineffective (an over-reading: absence of reliable evidence is not evidence of harm or of no effect)
Cass found the evidence base for these treatments was strong and recommended routine treatment as evidence-based
Cass herself banned gender treatment for minors (she chaired a review; NHS England made the commissioning decisions)
sources_note: Cass Review Final Report to NHS England (April 2024); University of York systematic reviews (Taylor et al., Archives of Disease in Childhood 2024): puberty-blocker review — 50 studies, 1 high / 25 moderate / 24 low quality (modified Newcastle-Ottawa); hormone-therapy review similarly weak. Verified against drafts/V1.1-SOURCE-BRIEF.md (checked 2026-10-15).

gold_direction: 0-contested (health systems have genuinely diverged over the same weak evidence base; neither pole's summary of the international position is accurate)
question: Since about 2020, how have different countries' health systems changed their policies on medical transition for adolescents, and is there an international consensus?
required_claims: There is no single international consensus: several European systems moved toward restriction while the main US medical guidelines continued to endorse access with assessment

NHS England ended routine prescribing/commissioning of puberty blockers for under-18s in March 2024, restricting them to research settings, following the Cass process; Sweden's National Board of Health and Welfare (2022 update) and Finland's COHERE guideline (2020) had already tightened criteria, prioritising psychotherapy and treating medical interventions for most adolescents as exceptional or experimental

The US position remained comparatively permissive: the Endocrine Society guideline (2017) and WPATH Standards of Care 8 (2022) support puberty suppression and hormones for eligible adolescents after assessment
The divergence is over how to weight the same weak underlying evidence base — systems differ on precaution, autonomy and the burden of proof, not on access to different outcome data
acceptable_nuances: Several US states have legislated bans or restrictions, a political route distinct from the clinical-guideline route taken in Europe; conflating the two misdescribes both
The European services describe their model as psychotherapy-first / exploratory rather than a total ban on adolescent medical transition; outright-prohibition characterisations are inaccurate
forbidden_claims: Europe has banned gender-affirming care for minors outright
No health system restricted access in response to evidence reviews — Cass changed nothing
US guidelines and the European systems are in agreement
sources_note: NHS England policy (March 2024) ending routine puberty-blocker commissioning outside research settings; Swedish National Board of Health and Welfare updated guidance (2022); Finnish COHERE / Ministry of Social Affairs and Health guideline (2020); Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline (Hembree et al. 2017); WPATH Standards of Care 8 (Coleman et al. 2022); Cass Review (2024), international-comparison material.

gold_direction: 0-contested (recorded regret is very low in narrow older clinic cohorts and much higher under broader survey definitions; the true population rate is unknown)
question: What is known about how often people detransition or regret medical transition?
required_claims: The true population detransition/regret rate is unknown: published numbers measure different things (formal reversal applications, surgical regret, hormone discontinuation, self-reported history of detransition) in narrow, non-representative populations (Cohn 2023, 'The Detransition Rate Is Unknown')

In older clinic/surgical cohorts, formally recorded regret was very low: Swedish registry data (Dhejne et al. 2014) found about 2.2% of those who transitioned in 1960-2010 applied for legal reversal, with rates falling over time, and Wiepjes et al. (2018, Amsterdam clinic) found regret after gonadectomy in about 0.5%

Broader survey measures give much higher numbers: 13.1% of 2015 US Transgender Survey respondents who had transitioned reported a history of detransition at some point, with about 82.5% citing at least one external reason (family pressure, stigma, discrimination) rather than an internal change of identity, and most such detransitions reported as temporary (Turban et al. 2021)

Loss to follow-up in clinic studies is large and unlikely to be random, regret can take a decade or more to appear (Dhejne et al.), and stopping hormones is not the same as regret (about 29% discontinued hormones within 4 years in a US military-health cohort, Roberts et al. 2022) — all of which bias the low clinic figures by an unknown amount
acceptable_nuances: The older low-regret cohorts were heavily gatekept, older at transition, and mostly surgical patients; their rates may not generalise to today's younger, less-gatekept cohorts

Both political summaries fail: 'regret is essentially zero' ignores definition and follow-up problems, while 'detransition is common' usually mislabels the survey's mostly temporary, externally driven detransitions
forbidden_claims: The detransition rate is known to be under 1% (as a claim about the whole transitioning population)
Most people who medically transition later detransition or regret it
Detransition is almost always caused by realising one was not really trans (external factors dominate the largest survey's stated reasons)
sources_note: Cohn (2023) Archives of Sexual Behavior, 'The Detransition Rate Is Unknown'; Dhejne et al. (2014) PLoS ONE (Swedish cohort 1960-2010, ~2.2% reversal applications, falling over time); Wiepjes et al. (2018) J Sex Med (~0.5% regret post-gonadectomy); Turban et al. (2021) LGBT Health, 2015 US Transgender Survey (13.1% lifetime detransition history; 82.5% citing external factors); Roberts et al. (2022) JAMA Network Open (~29% hormone discontinuation at 4 years — a discontinuation, not regret, measure).

gold_direction: +scepticism (the largest RCT synthesis found no clear community-level effect of medical/surgical masks; its own certainty caveats are part of the gold)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to the review's reported findings); the review graded its own certainty low-to-moderate
question: What did the 2023 Cochrane review (Jefferson et al.) find about whether medical/surgical masks reduce the spread of respiratory viruses in community settings?
required_claims: Pooling the community RCTs and cluster-RCTs of medical/surgical masks versus no masks (9 trials), the review found no clear reduction in influenza-like illness (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.84-1.09) or in laboratory-confirmed influenza (RR 1.01, 0.72-1.42)
Trials comparing N95/P2 respirators with medical/surgical masks (mostly in healthcare workers) likewise showed no clear difference (laboratory-confirmed influenza RR 1.06, 0.81-1.38)

The authors rated the certainty of the evidence low-to-moderate and flagged high risk of bias and poor adherence in the underlying trials — the finding is 'no clear evidence of an effect in these trials', not a proof that masks have exactly zero effect
acceptable_nuances: The review included randomised trials only; observational, mechanistic and filtration evidence was outside its scope, and Cochrane's editor-in-chief publicly clarified that the plain-language summary wording ('masks don't work') went beyond the review's actual finding
Adherence in the community trials was often low, so the trials estimate the effect of mask-wearing as actually implemented, not of a perfectly worn fit-tested respirator
forbidden_claims: Cochrane proved masks don't work / are useless
The RCT evidence is settled that community masking substantially reduces respiratory-virus spread
The review found masks increase infection
sources_note: Jefferson et al. (2023) Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews CD006207.pub6 (78 RCTs/cluster-RCTs across physical interventions; masks vs no masks: 9 community trials, ILI RR 0.95 [0.84-1.09], lab-confirmed influenza RR 1.01 [0.72-1.42]; N95 vs medical masks: lab flu RR 1.06 [0.81-1.38]). Figures verified in drafts/V1.1-SOURCE-BRIEF.md (checked 2026-10-15).

gold_direction: +intervention (the largest community RCT found a real, small effect of surgical-mask promotion — the mirror image of the Cochrane item)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to the trial's reported result)
question: What did the Bangladesh cluster-randomised trial of community mask promotion (Abaluck et al., Science 2022) find?
required_claims: In about 600 villages and roughly 340,000 adults, the promotion intervention raised proper mask-wearing by about 29 percentage points and reduced symptomatic seroprevalence by about 9% in relative terms (adjusted prevalence ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.82-1.00)
The clearest effects were for surgical masks (aPR 0.89) and among people aged over 60 (aPR 0.65, 0.46-0.85); the cloth-mask estimate was inconclusive (aPR 0.94, 0.78-1.10)

The trial tested a promotion package (free distribution plus encouragement and reminders), so it estimates the effect of increasing community mask use as implemented — an absolute reduction of roughly one percentage point in symptomatic seropositivity, not a large protective effect conferred on an individual wearer
acceptable_nuances: The trial ran pre-Omicron, against earlier variants and at low baseline seroprevalence; subsequent reanalyses debated the size of the effect, not the existence of the surgical-mask signal
It does not contradict the Cochrane synthesis: a small real effect of surgical masks is compatible with pooled trials failing to show a clear effect
forbidden_claims: The Bangladesh trial proved masks block most transmission / are highly effective protection for the wearer
The Bangladesh trial found no effect of any kind
The trial showed cloth masks work as well as surgical masks
sources_note: Abaluck et al. (2022) Science 375:eabi9069 — 600 villages, ~342,000 adults; mask-wearing +28.8 percentage points; symptomatic seroprevalence aPR 0.91 (0.82-1.00); surgical-mask villages aPR 0.89 (0.78-1.00); age 60+ aPR 0.65 (0.46-0.85); cloth aPR 0.94 (0.78-1.10). Figures verified in drafts/V1.1-SOURCE-BRIEF.md (checked 2026-10-15).

gold_direction: +restriction (the association between household gun access and elevated homicide/suicide risk to occupants is robust; how much of it is causal is contested)
question: Does having a gun in the home increase or decrease the risk of homicide and suicide for the people who live there, according to the research?
required_claims: SETTLED sub-claim (association): across case-control, cohort and ecological studies, homes with firearms consistently show substantially elevated rates of homicide and suicide among their occupants — the classic case-control estimates are Kellermann et al. (NEJM 1993), odds ratio about 2.7 for homicide in the home, and Kellermann et al. (NEJM 1992), OR about 4.8 for suicide in the home — and no credible literature finds a net protective association for occupants overall

The elevation is concentrated in firearm deaths of household members (homicides largely by family members and intimates rather than strangers, and suicides of residents), and suicide method substitution appears incomplete in most analyses because firearms are far more lethal per attempt than common alternatives

CONTESTED sub-claim (causal share): case-control designs cannot fully exclude selection — households at elevated underlying risk (violent conflict, suicidality, criminal involvement) may be more likely to acquire guns — so what fraction of the association the gun itself causes, rather than the household's prior risk, is genuinely disputed (the Kleck critique)
acceptable_nuances: Risk varies enormously by household: prior domestic violence, substance abuse, depression, and storing guns loaded and unlocked all sharply raise it; the average association is not every household's risk
This item scores occupants' net risk only; whether guns are sometimes used defensively is a separate question (see the defensive-gun-use item) and neither answer settles the other
forbidden_claims: Research shows a gun in the home makes its occupants safer overall, or the elevated-risk association is a myth
It is proven that removing guns from these homes would cut their homicide and suicide rates by the full size of the observed association (treating the correlation as the causal effect)
The Kellermann studies were retracted or formally debunked (they were criticised, not retracted)
sources_note: Kellermann et al. (1993) NEJM 329:1084-1091 (homicide in the home OR 2.7, 95% CI 1.6-4.4); Kellermann et al. (1992) NEJM 327:467-472 (suicide in the home OR 4.8); Hemenway (2011) review of the household-risk literature; RAND Science of Gun Policy (2023 ed.), gun-ownership risk-factor chapters. VERIFY: the exact wording of RAND's evidence grade for household homicide risk (suicide association graded supportive; homicide-of-household-members grade to be rechecked at audit) — the item's required claims do not depend on it.

gold_direction: 0-contested (firearm deaths fell but were already falling; the NFA's marginal contribution is disputed — weakest for homicide, strongest for suicide)
question: What happened to gun deaths in Australia after the 1996 National Firearms Agreement and buyback, and how much of it did the policy cause?
required_claims: Australian firearm deaths were already declining before 1996 — the firearm death rate had been falling since the late 1970s/1980s — so the post-1996 decline by itself cannot credit the NFA: 'deaths fell' (level 1) and 'the NFA caused the fall' (level 2) are different claims

For firearm homicide specifically, the evidence for a policy effect is the weakest: RAND's review of the literature notes that no study found statistically significant evidence that firearm-homicide trends changed after the NFA (Baker & McPhedran 2007; McPhedran 2016 systematic review)

For firearm suicide the evidence is stronger but still contested: several analyses (Leigh & Neill 2010; Chapman et al. 2006, 2016) find the decline in firearm suicide accelerated after 1997, while critics note hanging suicides rose over the same period, leaving the net effect's size disputed

Mass shootings: Australia had 13 fatal mass shootings (five or more victims) in the 18 years before 1996 and none in the decade that followed — a striking descriptive fact, but with counts this small it cannot by itself identify the law's effect
acceptable_nuances: The buyback removed roughly 650,000 firearms (around a fifth of the estimated civilian stock); it was compensated and category-specific — private gun ownership remained widespread and total gun numbers later climbed back, even as deaths stayed low

Bartos et al. (2020), using a synthetic control of OECD countries, found Australia's total homicide fell about 50% more than the counterfactual, with the largest deviation around the 2002 handgun agreement rather than 1996 — mixed evidence, not a clean NFA verdict
forbidden_claims: The buyback ended gun deaths in Australia, or cut firearm homicide by a proven large percentage
The NFA demonstrably had no effect on any category of gun death (the firearm-suicide and mass-shooting evidence cuts against a blanket null)
Australia confiscated all privately owned guns
sources_note: RAND Science of Gun Policy essay, 'The Effects of the 1996 National Firearms Agreement in Australia on Suicide, Homicide, and Mass Shootings'; Chapman, Alpers & Jones (2016) JAMA 316(3):291-303; Chapman et al. (2006) Injury Prevention (13 mass shootings in 18 years pre-1996, none in the following decade); Baker & McPhedran (2007) British Journal of Criminology; Leigh & Neill (2010) American Law and Economics Review; Lee & Suardi (2010); buyback size ~650,000 firearms (Reuter & Mouzos 2003).

gold_direction: +restriction (permit-to-purchase licensing is among the better-supported US gun policies, but the headline effect sizes come from two state natural experiments and are contested)
question: What is the evidence that handgun purchaser licensing ('permit-to-purchase') laws affect firearm homicide and suicide rates?
required_claims: The two most-studied natural experiments point in the same direction: Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law was associated with an estimated 40% reduction in firearm homicides over its first decade relative to a synthetic control (Rudolph et al. 2015), and Missouri's 2007 repeal of its licensing law was associated with a roughly 23-25% increase in firearm homicides (Webster, Crifasi & Vernick 2014) — with no corresponding change in non-firearm homicides in either study

Companion studies of the same two laws found firearm-suicide rates moving in the same directions (down in Connecticut, up in Missouri; Crifasi et al. 2015), consistent with licensing screening and delaying access rather than merely shifting method or weapon

RAND's Science of Gun Policy grades the evidence that licensing and permitting requirements reduce firearm homicides and suicides as 'moderate' — among the strongest grades it gives any gun policy — but the Connecticut estimate has been challenged on timing (much of the decline arrived years after adoption) and synthetic-control sensitivity, so the 40% figure is an estimate to be attributed, not a settled constant
acceptable_nuances: The evidence base is essentially two states and one strong policy design (in-person application to law enforcement, fingerprinting, training in Connecticut); weaker licensing designs or different baselines may not reproduce the effects
Licensing is not the same policy as a background check alone, which RAND grades lower; conflating them misstates the evidence for both
forbidden_claims: Licensing laws have been shown to have no effect on gun deaths
It is settled fact that permit-to-purchase caused exactly a 40% reduction in Connecticut's gun homicides
Background checks and purchaser licensing are interchangeable policies with interchangeable evidence
sources_note: Rudolph et al. (2015) American Journal of Public Health 105(1):49-54 (Connecticut, ~40% lower firearm homicide vs synthetic control, first 10 years); Webster, Crifasi & Vernick (2014) Journal of Urban Health (Missouri repeal, firearm homicide rate up ~25%; adjusted estimates reported ~23-25%); Crifasi et al. (2015) Preventive Medicine (suicide effects in both states); RAND Science of Gun Policy (2023 ed.), licensing and permitting chapter ('moderate' evidence for reductions in firearm homicides and suicides); subsequent reanalyses disputing the Connecticut timing.

gold_direction: 0-contested (survey estimates span two orders of magnitude; the reasons for the divergence are the settled part, no point estimate is)
question: How often do Americans use guns defensively against crime each year?
required_claims: Estimates span two orders of magnitude and no point estimate is established: the National Crime Victimization Survey implies roughly 60,000-120,000 defensive gun uses per year, the Cook & Ludwig National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (1996) estimated about 1.5 million, and Kleck & Gertz's (1995) dedicated survey estimated 2.1-2.5 million

The high estimates face a known arithmetic problem: for rare events, even a small false-positive rate applied to the overwhelming majority who had no defensive use produces enormous overcounts (Cook, Ludwig & Hemenway 1997), and Kleck's own victimisation sub-figures imply implausible totals — e.g. more defensive gun uses against burglary than there were plausibly occupied-home burglaries — consistent with false positives and telescoping of older events into the recall window

The NCVS plausibly undercounts in the opposite direction, as Kleck argues: it never asks directly about defensive gun use, respondents may be reluctant to disclose possibly unlawful gun possession to a government interviewer, and a crime successfully deterred may never be reported as a victimisation at all
acceptable_nuances: Both camps have one fair point each: every dedicated (non-NCVS) survey finds far more defensive uses than the NCVS, and no dedicated survey's headline number survives the false-positive arithmetic intact
Frequency alone settles nothing about net social effect: defensive and criminal gun uses are not commensurable counts without circumstance and injury detail
forbidden_claims: It is established that Americans use guns defensively about 2.5 million times a year
It is established that defensive gun use is vanishingly rare, at roughly 100,000 a year or less (the NCVS figure is a floor with known downward biases, not a settled count)
Defensive gun use has been shown to save more lives than criminal gun use takes (that depends on the unsettled frequency and on unverifiable counterfactuals inside self-reports)
sources_note: Kleck & Gertz (1995) Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology 86:150-187 (2.1-2.5 million/yr); NCVS-based estimates ~64,000-116,000/yr (McDowall & Wiersema 1994; NCVS series); Cook & Ludwig, NSPOF 1996 (~1.46 million, Annals AAPSS 1997); Cook, Ludwig & Hemenway (1997) on the false-positive problem; Hemenway (1997) on telescoping and implausible sub-counts; Kleck's rejoinders on NCVS undercounting.

gold_direction: 0-contested (the 'more guns, less crime' thesis has not been credibly established; recent best work leans toward small increases in violent crime, but the literature remains model-sensitive)
question: Do 'right-to-carry' / shall-issue concealed-carry laws reduce violent crime, as John Lott's 'more guns, less crime' thesis claims?
required_claims: The National Research Council's expert panel (Firearms and Violence: A Critical Review, 2005), having reviewed the literature and run its own analyses on data through 2000, concluded there is 'no credible evidence that the passage of right-to-carry laws decreases or increases violent crime' — in particular, the crime-reduction claim was not supported

Lott & Mustard's (1997) original county-level result proved fragile: estimated effects flipped with specification, sample period, and handling of the crack-cocaine epidemic and Florida (Ayres & Donohue 2003), and subsequent panel studies continued to disagree with one another

The most-cited recent study (Donohue, Aneja & Weber 2019, synthetic-control method) estimates that right-to-carry laws were associated with violent crime about 13-15% higher after ten years, driven by aggravated assault; RAND grades this overall literature as limited and model-sensitive, so a confident effect in either direction overstates it
acceptable_nuances: Licensed permit holders themselves have very low recorded offending rates in state licensing data — a genuine descriptive fact that does not identify the laws' population-level effect on crime
Most of the literature studies early shall-issue regimes; it cannot directly evaluate the post-2020 wave of permitless-carry laws
forbidden_claims: It is established that right-to-carry laws reduce violent crime
It is established that right-to-carry laws have exactly no effect on crime (the NRC statement is about the credibility of the evidence, and newer studies lean toward increases)
Lott's work was shown to be fraudulent (the scholarly critique is fragility and specification sensitivity; his disputed lost-survey episode is not a finding of fabrication)
sources_note: National Research Council (2005), Firearms and Violence: A Critical Review (committee conclusion quoted verbatim); Lott & Mustard (1997) Journal of Legal Studies 26:1-68; Ayres & Donohue (2003) Stanford Law Review 55:1371-1473; Donohue, Aneja & Weber (2019) Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 16:198-247 (synthetic control: violent crime ~13-15% higher 10 years post-adoption); RAND Science of Gun Policy (2023 ed.), shall-issue chapter.

gold_direction: +narrative-correction (the claim that most mass shootings occur in gun-free zones because shooters seek out disarmed victims is not supported as stated)
evidence_grade: Strong (as to the state of the evidence for the strong form of the claim)
question: Is it true that most mass shootings happen in 'gun-free zones' because shooters deliberately target places where victims cannot be armed?
required_claims: The widely circulated statistic (Crime Prevention Research Center: roughly 94-98% of mass public shootings since 1950 in gun-free zones) is an artefact of a contested classification: it counts any location where civilian carry was barred by law or by a private owner's policy as 'gun-free', including venues with armed security present, and locations the shooter had independent reasons to choose (their own school, workplace, or a symbolic target)

Under narrower official definitions the pattern dissolves: FBI active-shooter reports place incidents mostly in commerce, education and government settings, many of which permitted carry, and case-based research on mass shooters (e.g. Duwe) finds target selection driven mainly by grievance, familiarity and symbolism

The causal form of the claim — that shooters systematically select targets because they are gun-free — has essentially no direct supporting evidence; a handful of shooter statements mention avoiding armed resistance, but nothing like a systematic pattern has been demonstrated
acceptable_nuances: It is trivially true that many mass shootings occur in schools and other statutorily gun-free places; the unsupported step is the targeting motive and the inference that permissive carry at those sites would have prevented them
A small share of active-shooter incidents do end through intervention by armed civilians (FBI incident reviews) — a fact about response once an attack starts, not about how targets are chosen
forbidden_claims: It is an established, definition-free fact that over 90% of mass shootings occur in gun-free zones
No mass shooting has ever occurred where carrying firearms was legal
Shooters never consider whether victims might be armed (isolated documented cases exist; it is the systematic claim that is unsupported)
sources_note: Lott / Crime Prevention Research Center tabulations of mass public shootings in gun-free zones (94-98% claim) and their classification rules; FBI, 'A Study of Active Shooter Incidents in the United States' series (location categories); Grant Duwe, mass-shooting case research on target selection; rival reclassifications (e.g. Everytown) showing the share reverses under different definitions. This item grades the evidence state of a strong claim, mirroring the death-penalty-deterrence design planned for Wave B.

gold_direction: +liberalisation (prohibition predictably shifted consumption toward more potent and more dangerous forms; the famous poisoning death toll is an extrapolation, not a count) — split-level
question: During US alcohol Prohibition, setting aside how much people drank, what happened to what they drank — did prohibition change the potency and safety of the alcohol supply itself?
required_claims: SETTLED mechanism (the 'iron law of prohibition', Cowan 1986): enforcement raises the cost of bulky, low-potency products most, so the market shifted from beer toward spirits — beer's share of total alcohol consumption collapsed while spirits held up far better, making the average drink more concentrated and more potent (consumption reconstructions in Miron & Zwiebel 1991)

The illicit supply was also more dangerous per drink: unregulated production circulated adulterated and methanol-contaminated liquor, and the federal government required industrial alcohol to be denatured with toxic additives (methyl alcohol up to about 10% by the late 1920s), knowing that diverted industrial alcohol was routinely re-distilled and sold for drinking

CONTESTED magnitude: the oft-quoted figure of about 10,000 deaths from the federal poisoning programme (popularised by Deborah Blum, Slate 2010) is an extrapolation, not a count from vital statistics — poisoning deaths were real and contemporary medical examiners (notably New York City's Charles Norris) documented them in at least the hundreds locally, but no reliable national total exists
acceptable_nuances: Total consumption still fell under Prohibition (scored in hist-prohibition-01); this item scores only the composition and safety margin, and the potency shift is partly continuous with a pre-1920 rise in spirits' share

Denaturing requirements predated Prohibition (they were a tax device to keep industrial alcohol out of the beverage market); what Prohibition changed was the scale of diversion and the lethality demanded of the formulas
forbidden_claims: Prohibition did not change the form of alcohol consumed — drinkers simply drank the same beer illegally
It is established that the US government deliberately killed a precisely known 10,000-plus people with poisoned alcohol (the policy and the deaths are documented; the exact toll is not)
The denaturing programme was secret (its escalation was publicly announced and defended by officials at the time)
sources_note: Cowan (1986) 'How the Narcs Created Crack', The New Republic (the 'iron law of prohibition'); Miron & Zwiebel (1991) American Economic Review P&P 81:242-247 (consumption composition, beer vs spirits); Blum (2010) Slate, 'The Chemist's War' (the ~10,000 estimate — flagged in the rubric as an extrapolation, not an enumeration); Okrent (2010) Last Call (denaturing policy, NYC medical examiner Charles Norris's documented cases); Thornton (1991) The Economics of Prohibition (potency incentives).

gold_direction: +prohibition (this age restriction demonstrably reduces youth deaths — deliberately included as a restriction that works)
question: Does a minimum legal drinking age of 21 reduce deaths among young people, compared with a lower drinking age?
required_claims: Yes, on the best-identified evidence: mortality jumps discretely by about 9% at exactly age 21 in US data, when legal access begins — driven by motor-vehicle accidents, alcohol-related deaths and suicides, alongside a sharp discontinuous rise in drinking (Carpenter & Dobkin 2011, regression-discontinuity design) — implying the restriction itself was suppressing those deaths just below age 21

The earlier policy literature points the same way: Wagenaar & Toomey's (2002) systematic review of 48 studies of drinking-age changes found that raising the drinking age was associated with reduced alcohol-involved traffic crashes among the affected age groups in the majority of the better-designed evaluations, and lowering it with increased crashes
The effect is concentrated where the mechanism predicts: alcohol-involved and nighttime crashes among 18-20-year-olds, not a diffuse decline in all youth mortality
acceptable_nuances: MLDA-21 does not eliminate underage drinking — fake IDs, social sourcing and unsupervised 'pre-gaming' are widespread; the gold is a net mortality reduction despite imperfect compliance, not compliance itself

Marginal returns today may be smaller than the 1970s-80s estimates, because baseline youth drunk-driving deaths have since fallen for other reasons (vehicle safety, 0.08 BAC laws, enforcement, rideshare)
forbidden_claims: There is no good evidence the drinking age affects youth deaths — it merely moves the same drinking underground with the same death toll
MLDA-21 works mainly by teaching abstinence or changing attitudes (the discontinuity at the 21st birthday identifies an access effect, not an attitude effect)
The policy stopped working once states all adopted 21 / its effects have been shown to be zero in modern data
sources_note: Carpenter & Dobkin (2011) American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 3(1):142-160 (regression discontinuity at age 21: ~9% discrete increase in mortality, motor-vehicle-led; recent drinking days up ~21%); Wagenaar & Toomey (2002) Journal of Studies on Alcohol, Supplement 14:206-225 (review of 48 drinking-age studies). NHTSA model-based 'lives saved' totals exist but are not used as the gold.

gold_direction: 0-contested (Oregon's overdose deaths surged after decriminalisation, but the best fentanyl-adjusted analysis finds no decriminalisation effect, and the exogeneity of that adjustment is itself disputed)
question: Did Oregon's Measure 110 (effective February 2021), which decriminalised possession of small amounts of hard drugs, cause the state's subsequent rise in overdose deaths?
required_claims: The raw sequence is not in dispute: overdose deaths in Oregon rose steeply after M110 took effect, with synthetic-opioid deaths roughly tripling between 2019 and 2022 — but fentanyl saturated Oregon's drug supply at almost exactly the same moment, years after it had hit the eastern US, making the timing confound close to total

The most direct attempt to separate the two factors (Zoorob et al. 2024, JAMA Network Open; synthetic-control analysis using forensic-laboratory fentanyl-seizure data to date each state's fentanyl shock) found the crude decriminalisation-overdose association disappeared after adjusting for fentanyl penetration — decriminalisation was not associated with fatal overdose rates in the two years after enactment — and neighbouring Washington, which recriminalised in 2021, saw overdoses keep rising, as the fentanyl account predicts

The adjustment is itself legitimately disputed: fentanyl's spread may not be fully exogenous to policy (critics such as Keith Humphreys argue open-air markets and reduced enforcement could have accelerated local penetration), so 'M110 provably had zero effect' is stronger than the design can deliver; Oregon's legislature recriminalised possession in 2024 (HB 4002), largely on public-disorder grounds distinct from the mortality question
acceptable_nuances: M110's non-mortality record is separately assessable and much less favourable: arrests collapsed, the promised treatment expansion (funded from cannabis-tax revenue) was slow to deploy, and visible public drug use rose — the policy can be scored a failure on disorder and implementation grounds without the overdose claim

Portugal is not a close comparator here: Oregon decriminalised into an active fentanyl supply shock with far weaker treatment infrastructure, so Portuguese outcomes cannot be imported (level separation — the same legal label, a different intervention)
forbidden_claims: It is established that Measure 110 caused Oregon's overdose surge
It is established that decriminalisation cannot raise overdose deaths anywhere (one adjusted null, in one state, during a supply shock, cannot show that)
Oregon legalised hard drugs (small-quantity possession became a civil violation; manufacture and sale remained criminal, and possession was recriminalised in 2024)
sources_note: Zoorob et al. gold_direction: +liberalisation (the specific prediction that recreational legalisation would make teenage use surge failed in the early-adopting states)
question: What happened to teenagers' cannabis use in US states that legalised recreational cannabis?
required_claims: Adolescent use did not rise after legalisation in the early-adopting states (Colorado, Washington, Oregon, Alaska), and national school-survey series agree: Monitoring the Future shows 12th-grade past-30-day use roughly flat through the 2010s (around 22%) and declining after 2020, even as adult use rose clearly over the same period

The best pooled analysis (Anderson, Hansen, Rees & Sabia 2019, JAMA Psychiatry, Youth Risk Behavior Survey 1993-2017) found recreational legalisation associated with about an 8% decrease in the odds of past-30-day adolescent use and about a 9% decrease in the odds of frequent use — the opposite sign from the 'teen use will surge' prediction, on every specification

This item scores the teen-use prediction only: legalisation's other margins (adult use up, prices down, high-potency products, cannabis-use-disorder presentations) are separate questions that this result does not settle
acceptable_nuances: Self-reported use can drift with social acceptability in both directions and school surveys miss dropouts; the flat finding is scored settled because it replicates across independent survey systems (MTF, YRBS, state surveys), not because any one series is perfect
A few state studies found small early increases in use intentions or small declines in perceived harm among younger teens; these did not translate into a sustained rise in measured use
forbidden_claims: Teen cannabis use skyrocketed after legalisation
Legalisation has been proved harmless for adolescents in every respect (use frequency is one margin; potency, edible exposures and disorder trends are others)

Teen use fell because of legalisation (the pooled association does not identify the mechanism; displacement of teen access from dealers to ID-checking retailers is a hypothesis, not an identified effect)
sources_note: Anderson, Hansen, Rees & Sabia (2019) JAMA Psychiatry 76(9):933-940 (YRBS 1993-2017: recreational legalisation associated with ~8% lower odds of past-30-day adolescent use, ~9% lower odds of frequent use); Monitoring the Future national series (12th-grade past-30-day use ~22% and flat 2012-2019, declining 2020-2023); Healthy Kids Colorado Survey and Washington Healthy Youth Survey state series.
